title: The Fried Liver Attack
description: This course teaches you the famous Fried Liver Attack out of the Italian Game. And as a bonus, you learn how to play a regular aggressive Italian after 3...Bc5. A great repertoire for beginners and intermediate players.

r1b2b1r/pp2k1pp/2p2q2/3np3/1nBP4/2N5/PPP.text:
Let's check out the top engine line. 11...Ke7 is played very rarely, 10% of the games went like this.

We keep our foot on the gas pedal: the knight jumps to e4, where it is very active.

r1b2b1r/pp2k1pp/2p3q1/3np3/1nBPN3/8/PPP1.text:
Black sidesteps the attack and prepares ...Bf5.

c2-c3 supports the pawn on d4 and attacks the b4-knight.

r1b2b1r/pp2k1pp/8/q2BP3/8/5Q2/PP3PPP/n1B.text:
Black retreats.

Now the queen invades the f7-square with check.

r1b2b1r/pp4pp/2p1kq2/3np3/1nBP4/2N2Q2/PP.text:
Nearly 30% of the time, Black offers a queen trade with 10...Qf6.

We decline, of course. Trading the queens would only help Black. White's queen can drop back to e2 where it continues to x-ray the king.

r1b2b1r/pp4pp/4k3/q2pP3/2B5/5Q2/PP3PPP/n.text:
Black moves away from the d-file pin.

We play Bxd5+! The king hunt begins.

r1b2b1r/ppp2kpp/2n2q2/3np3/2B5/5Q2/PPPP1.text:
In nearly 20% of the games Black blocks the check with their queen.

We can now grab our piece back with a check.

r1b4r/pp4pp/2pbk3/3n4/1nBqNP2/8/PPP1Q1PP.text:
...we'll step away to h1, where the king will be safe. 

Our plan still revolves around adding pressure to Black's pieces that are clustered in the center, with moves like Rd1 and c3, which threatens a fork.
Black captures on d4 with check...

r1b4r/pp4pp/2pbkq2/3n4/1nBPpP2/2N5/PPP1Q.text:
Black tries to close down the center as much as the can and open an attack on the d4-pawn.

We'll capture on e4; the knight on e4 is a very powerful piece anyway.

r1b4r/pp4pp/2pbkq2/3np3/1nBP4/2N5/PPP1QP.text:
Black gets the dark-squared bishop out.

We now add even more pressure to the center, with f4!, also aiming to open the f1-rook.

r1bk1b1r/pp3Qpp/8/q2BP3/8/8/PP3PPP/n1BR2.text:
The only legal move.

Now there is a checkmate in two moves, starting by bringing our last piece into the game!

r1bk3r/pp2Q1pp/8/q2BP1B1/8/8/PP3PPP/n2R2.text:
Checkmate! 

Going for the rook on a1 was a mistake by Black.

r1bk3r/pp2bQpp/8/q2BP1B1/8/8/PP3PPP/n2R2.text: Black must block with the bishop.

r1bq1b1r/pp4pp/2p1k3/3nP3/2B5/2N2Q2/PP3P.text:
80% of the time Black went for the material.

Now we grab the knight. Black doesn't have enough resources to defend it.

r1bq1b1r/pp4pp/2p1k3/3np3/1nB5/2N2Q2/PPP.text:
Black supports the knight on d5, which is the most popular continuation, occured 80% of the time.

It is time to play d4, looking to open up the center and open lines for our minor pieces and the rooks.

r1bq1b1r/pp4pp/2p1k3/3np3/2BP4/2N2Q2/PPn.text:
In 40% of the games, Black grabs the pawn on c2 and attacks our rook.

We can completely ignore the material losses and continue our attack with dxe5!, continuing to open up the position. King safety is what decides this game.

r1bq1b1r/pp4pp/2pk4/4p3/3nB3/2N5/PPPP1PP.text:
We'll retreat to e4, keeping its activity. 

White has a comfortable position — pawn up and ongoing pressure against Black's weakened pawn.

We'll continue with moves like d3 to continue developing and castling to hide our king and bring the rook into the game.

r1bq1b1r/pp4pp/4k3/3pP3/2B5/5Q2/PP3PPP/n.text:
Black recaptures.

Now, we increase the pressure by pinning the pawn to the queen on d8, while bringing our rook into the game.

r1bq1b1r/ppp1k1pp/8/3Bp3/3n4/2N2Q2/PPPP1.text:
In 24% of the games, Black retreats the king to e7.

This allows our queen to invade f7 with check.

r1bq1b1r/ppp2Qpp/3k4/3Bp3/3n4/2N5/PPPP1P.text: This is the only legal move.

r1bq1b1r/ppp2kpp/2n5/3np3/2B5/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
Black has to recapture since this comes with a double attack. Now that we've lured out Black's king to f7, the bishop's power increases as it pins the knight on d5. 

From now on, White's plan revolves around opening up the center and adding pressure to d5. We start by giving a check with Qf3, creating a double attack.

r1bq1b1r/ppp3pp/2n1k3/3np3/2B5/5Q2/PPPP1.text:
35% of games go like this: Black wants to defend their extra piece, but Black's king could find itself in danger.

We can start by developing a piece while adding more pressure to the pinned knight.

r1bq1b1r/ppp3pp/3k4/3Bp3/3n4/2N2Q2/PPPP1.text:
In 70% of the games, Black moves their king to d6.

White now tucks back the queen. It has done its job pressuring Black's king, so now it's time to defend the c2-pawn.

r1bq1b1r/ppp3pp/4k3/3Bp3/8/2N2Q2/PPnP1PP.text: We'll just capture the knight and continue the attack with moves like Bb3 and Ne4.

r1bq1b1r/ppp3pp/4k3/3np3/1nB5/2N2Q2/PPPP.text:
8...Nb4 is the second way that Black can go for when trying to deliver a fork on c2.

We'll castle here, preparing to get the rook into the action and getting our king into safety before opening up the center.

r1bq1b1r/ppp3pp/4k3/3np3/2B5/2N2Q2/PPnP1.text: Less than 10% of the games continue with 9...Nxc2.

r1bq1b1r/ppp3pp/4k3/3np3/2Bn4/2N2Q2/PPPP.text:
To counter our attacks, Black will usually try to deliver a fork on c2.

We can start by regain the piece back with a check.

r1bq1bkr/ppp3pp/2n5/3Bp3/8/5Q2/PPPP1PPP/.text: This leads to checkmate in two!

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pp1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.text:
This is the best move that Black can go for — blocking our bishop on c4. It's also the most popular, happening in 75% of amateur games.

We'll gladly take with our pawn, as it comes with a tempo on the c6-knight and might open up the diagonal to the f7-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3np1N1/2B5/8/PPPP1P.text:
As Black, most players are simply tempted to capture. 5...Nxd5 is the most popular move here. 

This allows for an aggressive continuation as White: we capture the pawn on f7, sacrificing the knight!

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n5/3Bp3/8/5Q2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
After we recapture on d5 with the bishop, Black's king is seriously weak and checkmate is already threatened. 

Here, a whopping 30% of the time, Black plays ...Nd4 to attack our queen and falls for the checkmate on f7!

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n5/3np3/2B5/5Q2/PPPP1PP.text: In 30% of the games, Black retreats their king back to e8, giving up the piece immediately, thinking they are safe.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
With 3...Nf6, Black is allowing the Fried Liver Attack. This move is tied in popularity with 3...Bc5, but the lower we go down the rating ladder, the more popular 3...Nf6 gets.

To enter the Fried Liver, we play 4.Ng5! We generally don't want to move the same piece twice, but in this case, White is threatening a dangerous fork on f7, which isn't defended easily if Black doesn't know what they're doing.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black also develops a knight while defending their pawn.

Now, 3.Bc4 is the signature move that signifies the Italian Game! The bishop on c4 immediately eyes the weak f7-pawn (only defended by Black's king).

r4b1r/p1p2kpp/2p1bq2/4p3/8/5Q2/PPPP1PPP/.text: Black recaptures, and now we recapture with the queen and attack c7.

r4b1r/pp2k1pp/2p3q1/3npb2/1nBPN3/2P5/PP2.text:
Black pressures our e4-knight.

We'll support it with f2-f3. In case Black decides to trade, we'll recapture and get the open f-file.

r4b1r/pp2k1pp/n1p3q1/3nPb2/2B1N3/2P2P2/P.text: And by grabbing the pawn on e5 we create an outpost on d6 and open up the d-file for our rook to put pressure on Black's king.

r4b1r/ppp2kpp/2n1bq2/3Bp3/8/5Q2/PPPP1PPP.text:
Black defends with the bishop.

We can win yet another pawn by capturing the knight first.

r4r2/p1p2kpp/2Qbbq2/4p3/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black aims to castle by hand.

d3 opens up our dark-squared bishop and add control over the e4-square.

r4rk1/p1p3pp/2Qbbq2/4p3/8/2NP4/PPP2PPP/R.text: Black gets their king into safety.

White castles here, getting the king into safety and after bringing out the bishop, connecting the rooks. 

We are up two pawns and a much better pawn structure.

r6r/p1p2kpp/2Qbbq2/4p3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB1.text:
Black defends c7 while developing.

It's time for us to start developing our remaining minor pieces as well, starting with Nc3, controlling the center and potentially eyeing the e4 square.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text: After 1.e4 e5, White will now develop their kingside knight and pressure the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the Fried Liver! 

In many cases, the classic e4-e5 and bringing the knights out tends to lead to a boring game, but in this course, you'll learn how to spice things up in the Italian!

First, let's examine the so-called "Fried Liver Attack," in which we pose serious threats to our opponent as early as on the fourth move. 

Let's check it out!

1rbqr1k1/p5pp/3b4/n2p1p2/3Pp3/5N2/PPP2PP.text: Trading would only benefit White, so Black decided to advance and take space.

1rbqr1k1/p5pp/3b4/n2pNp2/3Pp3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
The e5-square becomes a great outpost for our knight — since none of Black's pawns can attack it. A nice plan could be b3 with Bb2 fianchetto coming.

If Black decides to capture twice on e5, we would skewer them with Bf4, winning the exchange.

1rbqr1k1/p5pp/3b4/n2ppp2/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black occupies the b-file.

To counter Black's strong center, we expand with d4 and pose a question to the e5-pawn; do you want to trade or advance?

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/2pb4/n2np3/8/3B1N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black responds in a similar manner, which happens in most games.

Re1 now puts pressure on the e5-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/2pb4/n3p3/8/1PNP1N2/P2P1P.text:
With b3, White prepares to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop and occupy the e4-square with Ne4 and Re1. Eventually, White may be able to trade the weak d-pawn off with d3-d4.

This line was a part of a game between Fabiano Caruana and Hikaru Nakamura.

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/2pb4/n3p3/8/2NP1N2/PP1P1P.text: Black gets their king into safety.

r1bq1rk1/p5pp/2p5/n2nNp2/8/3B4/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Bf1 and d4 are solid ideas. 

If ...Re8 now, our knight can simply go back to f3.

In return for the exchange, we have an extra pawn, a healthy pawn structure, and clear development, and so White has good compensation.

r1bq1rk1/p5pp/2p5/n2nbp2/8/3B1N2/PPPP1PP.text:
You'll most probably see this simple recapture.

12...g5!? 13.Nc3 g4 14.Re1 is another crazy yet improbable line.

r1bq1rk1/p5pp/2pb4/n2npp2/8/3B1N2/PPPP1P.text:
The immediate ...f5, sacrificing the e5 pawn, is the computer's top choice. 12.Nxe5 leads to a crazy engine line, but we're not playing that.

Instead, we recommend 12.Rxe5!? This move has almost never been played.

r1bqk2r/p4pp1/2p4p/n1b1p3/4B3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
We get the king into safety. 

White can chose between two plans: 

a) c3 to push b4 and play Bc2 (or deflect the a5 knight and win c6 if Black allows it)

b) d3 with Bf3 and Nc3.
Black can now develop the bishop to c5.

r1bqk2r/p4ppp/2pb4/n2np3/8/3B1N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black supports the attacked pawn and prepares to castle.

By castling, we get the king into safety and prepare to invade the e-file with Re1 as well.

r1bqk2r/p4ppp/2pb4/n3p3/5n2/3B1N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black's knight jumps to f4, looking to take our bishop and double our pawns. This is also the main line at the top level.

White simply continues developing with 11.Nc3. The bishop has nowhere to go (Be4 runs into ...f5), but ...Nxd3 is not as bad for White as it may seem.

r1bqk2r/p4ppp/2pb4/n3p3/8/2Nn1N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black's idea is to play against the doubled d-pawns in the future, but White is equipped to defend the d-pawn with moves like Qe2.

Meanwhile, the pawn on d3 adds support to e4, and White has ideas of playing Re1 (pressuring e5) or Ne4 (blockading the e pawn).

r1bqkb1r/p4pp1/2p2n1p/n3p1N1/8/3B4/PPPP1.text:
Black poses a question to our knight, but this approach is slow. Our knight can return to the strong e4 square, where it stops Black's bishop from developing to c5.

The second most popular move at the top level is ...Ng4, to which we recommend the response Nh3, avoiding the complications of 9.Nf3 f5!?

r1bqkb1r/p4pp1/2p4p/n3p3/4n3/3B4/PPPP1PP.text: Black trades off our strong piece.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p2n2/nB2p1N1/8/8/PPPP1PP.text:
Black recaptures with the pawn. Here, White has many viable options, but in this course we recommend 8.Bd3.

The bishop on d3 nicely controls the e4-square, which functions an outpost for our knight.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p5/n2np1N1/8/3B4/PPPP1PP.text:
This is the second most popular move at the amateur level, with a 15% occurrence rate, but at the master level, it's the main line.

Black has opened up an attack on our g5-knight and has 2 approaches — immediate ...Nf4 after ...Bd6, or castling short.

We'll retreat the knight to f3, aiming to pressure the e5-pawn. Ne4?! is too slow, since Black is immediately infiltrating with ...Nf4!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/nB1Pp1N1/8/8/PPPP1.text:
Nearly 80% of the time, Black goes for this pawn sacrifice on c6.

After we accept with dxc6, we'll gain a pawn but have to deal with Black's increased activity.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pp1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.text:
This is the only move that interferes with our c4-bishop.

We'll gladly take with our pawn, as it comes with a tempo on the c6-knight and might open up the diagonal to the f7-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/n2Pp1N1/2B5/8/PPPP1.text:
The previous chapter looked at 5...Nxd5. In 40% of the games, Black goes for the top engine move, ...Na5.

It is important for Black to deal with our strong light-squared bishop on c4, which is attacking the f7-pawn.

Black's f6-knight is also attacking the pawn on d5, so we move the bishop out of danger with a check on b5, trying to hold on to the pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black plays 3...Nf6, attacking the e4 pawn. Unlike 3...Bc5, which is also very popular, this allows the Fried Liver Attack, since this move blocks the black queen's contact with the g5 square.

To enter the Fried Liver, we play 4.Ng5!, attacking f7, which is not easy to defend.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black also develops a knight while defending their pawn.

Now, 3.Bc4 is the signature move that signifies the Italian Game!

r1bqr1k1/p4ppp/2pb4/n2np3/8/3B1N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black defends the pawn with their rook.

Our other knight develops to c3 as usual. Note that if Black plays 12...Nxc3, we recapture with the d-pawn, opening up lines for our queen and bishop. We are up a pawn and are generally happy to make central trades.

r1bqr1k1/p5pp/2pb4/n2npp2/8/2NB1N2/PPPP1.text:
Black expands with ...f5, threatening a fork on e4.

White has less space and an extra pawn here, so trading pieces with Nxd5 is a good idea, even though we do give Black an imposing center.

r1bqr1k1/p5pp/3b4/n2ppp2/8/3B1N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black recaptures the piece.

We'll tuck the bishop back to f1, from where it plays a defensive role and can be unleashed later.

r2qk2r/pppb1ppp/3b1n2/nB1Pp1N1/8/8/PPPPQ.text:
Black ignores our plan and develops the dark-squared bishop.

We'll trade off the light-squared bishops to get rid of the tension between them and prevent Black from keeping them.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/5n2/nB1Pp1N1/8/8/PPPP1P.text:
In 17% of the games, Black blocks the check with the bishop on d7.

The key move for us is Qe2, supporting the bishop on b5, so in case Black trades, we'll recapture with check and get our queen to a more active square.

r3k2r/pppq1ppp/3b1n2/n2Pp1N1/8/2N5/PPPPQ.text:
The queenside knight finds itself on a natural c3-square, from where we defend the d5-pawn and control the e4-square. 

Moves like d3 and O-O will come, and White will have a very comfortable position.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Once again, we start with 1.e4 e5.

White will now develop their kingside knight and pressure the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the first study of chapter 2! 

Let's check out Black's second most popular fifth move, which is ...Na5. 

Although not as popular as 5...Nxd5, it is the engine's best choice, and deserves our attention.

Let's check it out!

1r1k1b1r/pbp2ppp/8/1B1np1q1/3P4/5Q2/PP1P.text:
Black defends the bishop on b7 so it is no longer hanging.

The x-ray on our queen is a bit scary, but we should start with dxe5. Black's position is close to being much worse. Their king is unsafe, and d2-d4 will open up a lot of lines for our pieces.

1r1k1b1r/pbp2ppp/8/1B2P1q1/8/4n2Q/PP1P1P.text: This is necessary, defending g2 and threatening a mate on d7. After 13...Qxg2+ 14.Qxg2 Nxg2, we play 15.d2-d4 with a small but significant advantage.

1r1k1b1r/pbp2ppp/8/1B2P1q1/8/4nQ2/PP1P1P.text: We allowed this wild move, hitting the rook and piling on g2.

r1b1kb1r/p1p2ppp/2n2n2/1Bq1p1N1/8/2N5/PP.text:
Only now do we slingshot back and capture on b5.

This position is suitable for moves like d3 to open up the dark-squared bishop and Qf3 to add pressure to the c6-knight.

r1b1kb1r/p1p2ppp/2n2n2/1p1qp1N1/8/8/PPPP.text:
Black grabs on d5, which happens in about 50% of the games.

However, since we have preemptively tucked away our bishop, we can now develop our knight with a tempo on the queen! 

Notice how the bishop on f1 nicely covers the g2-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/p1p2ppp/8/1p1np1q1/3P4/8/PP1P1P.text:
Black regains it by capturing on g5.

Now that Black's knight is no longer on d4, we can grab the pawn on b5 with a check!

r1bk1b1r/p1p2ppp/8/1B1np1q1/3P4/8/PP1P1P.text:
Black would lose the castling rights anyway (after ...Bd7), so they move the king to d8.

It's time to get our king into safety!

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2n2n2/1p1Pp1N1/2B5/8/PP.text:
5...b5 is also an interesting move that Black could go for, but it isn't played much, only 4% of the games continue like this. The idea is to lure out our bishop to b5 before capturing on d5.

Similar idea to the previous line, the bishop waits on f1 before capturing on b5!

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2n5/1p1np1N1/8/8/PPPP1P.text:
Close to 30% of the time, the pawn on d5 is recaptured with the knight, opening an attack onto g5.

However, we can capture on b5 *now*, counterattacking the c6-knight. Notice that Black can no longer play ...Qxd5.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/5n2/1p1Pp1N1/2Bn4/2P5/P.text:
Instead of retreating the knight, Black counter-attacks our bishop on c4. 7.cxd4?! bxc4 would yield an equal position where Black will eventually corral White's overextended pawns.

The best move is the classy Bf1!, retreating the bishop to a safe square. Black still has to deal with the hanging knight, and if that knight moves away from d4 now, we'll be able to capture on b5 with a check.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/8/1p1np1N1/3n4/2P5/PP1P.text:
A retreating knight move like ...Nf5 would be passive. Instead, Black goes for ...Nxd5, played in 75% of games. This move also opens up an attack on our knight.

We'll grab a piece on d4.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pp1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.text:
This is the only move that interferes with our c4-bishop.

We'll gladly take with our pawn, gaining a tempo on the c6-knight.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3Pp1N1/2Bn4/8/PPPP1.text:
Less than 10% of the time, Black choses to jump to the d4-square.

We should react immediately to kick it out with c3. If we play a slow move like O-O, Black can win back the pawn on d5 and have a pleasant position.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black plays 3...Nf6, attacking the e4 pawn. This allows the Fried Liver Attack.

To enter the Fried Liver, we play 4.Ng5!, attacking f7, which is not easy to defend.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black also develops a knight while defending their pawn.

Now, 3.Bc4 is the signature move that signifies the Italian Game!

r2k1b1r/pbp2ppp/8/1B1np1q1/3P4/8/PP1P1PP.text:
Black fianchettoes the light-squared bishop. This is a very key moment, as Black is on the verge of mating us with a combination like ...Ne3! and Qxg2#.

The only move that gives White an advantage is Qf3, pinning the knight on e4 to the bishop on b7, temporarily immobilizing Black's pieces.

r2q3r/p1pbb1pp/2n1k3/1B1np3/8/3P1Q2/PPP2.text:
Black defends the knight on d5. Note that ...Nf6 would lose to Bxc6.

We add pressure to the pinned knight with Nc3.

r2q3r/p1pbb1pp/2n1k3/1B2p3/8/2nP1Q2/PPP2.text:
Black trades it off.

Before recapturing, we can throw in Bc4+!, forcing the king to d6.

r2q3r/p1pbb1pp/2nk4/4p3/2B5/2PP1Q2/P1P2P.text: And after we recapture, Ba3+ and Qd5+ are both hard to cover as Black.

r2q3r/p1pbbkpp/2n5/1B1np3/8/3P4/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black must capture the knight, since it came with a fork.

Now Qf3+ comes with another double attack!

r2qk2r/p1pbbppp/2n5/1B1np1N1/8/3P4/PPP2P.text:
Black adds an attacker to the knight on g5, but suddenly the downside of ...Bd7 appears: the knight on d5 is loose.

Here comes a very surprising move: a sacrifice on f7! We lure the king out into the open.

r2qkb1r/p1pb1ppp/2n5/1B1np1N1/8/8/PPPP1P.text:
In more than half of the games, Black goes for ...Bd7, covering the knight on c7 and unpinning it at the same time.

We recommend the simple 8.d3, opening up the dark-squared bishop and fights for the e4-square.

r2qkb1r/pbp2ppp/2n5/1B1np1N1/8/3P4/PPP2P.text: We'll simply push d3, support the knight on g5, and castle on the next move.

r2qkb1r/pbp2ppp/2n5/1B1np1N1/8/8/PPPP1PP.text: This move is safer as Black but played less than 7...Bd7, around 40% of the games.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Once again, we start with 1.e4 e5.

White will now develop their kingside knight and pressure the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the second study! 

Let's check out other fifth moves that Black could go for after we capture the pawn on d5!

r1bq1r2/p1p1k1pp/2pp1n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PP.text:
Black recaptures on c6.

Now, Nf3! is a very useful move since we interfere with the rook on f8, which will cover our f2-pawn. We also avoid any possible discovery attacks on the unprotected g5-knight.

r1bq1r2/ppp1k1pp/2np1n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/8/PP.text:
Black opens up the c8-bishop by pushing ...d6.

We'll trade off the knight on c6 to prevent any defensive ideas by Black, such as ...Nc6-d4-e6.

r1bq1r2/ppppk1pp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/8/PPP.text:
This popular move is also the strongest. Black is starting to pile up on the f2-pawn.

By castling, we get the king out of the center and support f2 with the rook as well.

r1bq3r/ppppk1pp/2n5/2bnp1N1/4P3/8/PPPP1P.text:
Black decides to trade off the bishop, but this is hasty. White is practically winning now.

We start by recapturing with a tempo on the c6-knight.

r1bq3r/ppppk1pp/8/2bPp1N1/3n4/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
Black doesn't want to be passive, so they jump to the d4-square.

We kick the knight away again.

r1bq3r/ppppk1pp/8/2bPpnN1/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP.text:
And after we castle, the main advantage for White is Black's (non-existent) king safety. We also have an extra pawn!

The idea is to shred open the center with d4. In some lines, we may even kick out the knight on f5 with g2-g4.

r1bq3r/ppppkBpp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PPPP.text:
This first study covers the main line with ...Ke7, which has been played in 50% of games. It is a better move than ...Kf8, because one of Black's main sources of counterplay is ...Rf8.

It's time to retreat the bishop to d5, where it looks to eventually capture on c6, weakening Black's control over the center.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/8/P.text:
In the Traxler Counterattack, Black ignores the threat of Nxf7 and brings the bishop to c5, eyeing the soft f2-pawn. It's the second most popular move played in 13% of the games.

The best move here is Bxf7+! This forces Black to choose between ...Ke7 and ...Kf8. We do not recommend 5.Nxf7, where Black gets a massive initiative after Bxf2+!?.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black plays 3...Nf6, attacking the e4 pawn. This allows the Fried Liver Attack.

To enter the Fried Liver, we play 4.Ng5!, attacking f7, which is not easy to defend.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black also develops a knight while defending their pawn.

Now, 3.Bc4 is the signature move that signifies the Italian Game!

r2q1r2/p1p1k1pp/2pp1n2/2b1p3/4P1b1/3P1N2.text:
Now we simply start to develop our pieces, beginning with d3. We'll challenge Black's dark-squared bishop with Be3 and bring the knight to d2.

White is up a clean pawn and Black has lost castling rights, and their attack will run out of steam once we consolidate.

r2q1r2/p1p1k1pp/2pp1n2/2b1p3/4P1b1/5N2/P.text: Black pins us. Note that ...Nxe4? runs into d2-d4!, and Black is toast once the e-file opens. If White can deal with the knight on e4, they also have ideas of playing Bg5+, skewering the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Once again, we start with 1.e4 e5.

White will now develop their kingside knight and pressure the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In the third chapter, we'll examine a countergambit called the "Traxler". 

It's the second most popular response to the Fried Liver attack.

Black completely ignores the threat of Nxf7 and creates a counter-attack against our f-pawn.

Let's check it out!

r1b2k1r/ppp2Npp/2np4/4p3/4n2q/1B6/PPPP2P.text: It is easily covered with Qf1.

r1b2k1r/pppp1Np1/2n4p/4p3/4n2q/1B6/PPPP2.text: Black threatens a checkmate, but it's defended easily with Qf1!, lining our queen up with Black's king.

r1b4N/ppppk1p1/2n4p/4p3/4n2q/1B6/PPPP2PP.text:
And we just capture the rook on h8. 

Nobody is checkmating us anytime soon, meanwhile, we're ahead 7 points of material!

r1b4r/ppppkNp1/2n4p/4p3/4n2q/1B6/PPPP2PP.text: Black gets out of any discoveries.

r1bq1k1r/ppp2Npp/2np1n2/4p3/4P3/1B6/PPPP.text: Black again goes for the sacrifice on f2. We recapture, of course!

r1bq1k1r/ppp2Npp/2np4/4p3/4n3/1B6/PPPP1K.text:
Black grabs on e4 with check.

The same idea as with 6...h6 applies! Hide the king on g1 and leave room for the queen on f1.

r1bq1k1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/2bpp1N1/4P3/1B6/PP.text:
Black tries to play against our light-squared bishop by blocking its view. This move is played in 30% of the games.

We capture with our pawn, keeping the position open.

r1bq1k1r/ppp3pp/2n5/2bnp1N1/8/1B6/PPPP1P.text:
Black grabs it back, opening up an attack onto our knight on g5.

Now we bring the queen into the action and threaten a checkmate on f7!

r1bq1k1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/1B6/P.text:
...d6 aims to cover the light-squares by opening up the bishop on c8.

We'll still deliver a fork on f7!

r1bq1k1r/ppp4p/2n3p1/2bnp1NQ/8/1B6/PPPP1.text:
Black blocks our checkmate threat, but this opens a new diagonal to the king.

The queen can now invade with Qh6+!

r1bq1k1r/pppp1Bpp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PP.text:
Black goes for the bad second option, 5...Kf8. It looks safer, but disallows Black's whole plan of bringing the rook to f8 and counter-attacking us on f2.

Here, we retreat the bishop to b3, maintaining its strong diagonal. Unlike when Black played 5...Ke7, Bd5 wouldn't be good here, since Black has ...Nxd5 and our knight on g5 is hanging.

r1bq1k1r/pppp1Np1/2n2n1p/4p3/4P3/1B6/PPP.text: Black goes for their cheap tricks with ...Bxf2+, but we can just recapture.

r1bq1k1r/pppp1Np1/2n4p/4p3/4n3/1B6/PPPP1.text:
Black captures on e4 with a check.

The king is safe on g1 and we don't mind that the rook on h1 is closed, since we are winning ample material to make up for that. We also want to leave the f1 square available for our queen!

r1bq1k1r/pppp2p1/2n2n1p/2b1p1N1/4P3/1B6/.text:
The third most popular move 6...h6 is attacking our knight, which also isn't a great choice by our opponent.

We'll deliver the fork on f7! With the king on f8, there is no counterplay down the f-file to worry about.

r1bq1k1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/4p1N1/4P3/1B6/PPP.text:
This move is somehow the second most popular move, occurring in almost 20% of the games. 

Let's just say that it's not a good move. We can just grab the bishop without any worry.

r1bq1k1r/pppp2pp/2n5/4p1N1/4n3/1B6/PPPP1.text: Black thinks that they'll regain the piece...

r1bq1k1r/pppp2pp/2n5/4p3/4N3/1B6/PPPP1KP.text:
...but we can just capture on e4 with the knight and go for Rf1+ and Kg1 to get the king into safety.

Black has no counterplay here. Qh4+ is met with Ng3.

r1bqk2r/ppp4p/2n3pQ/2bnp1N1/8/1B6/PPPP1P.text: Black moves the king to f8, not allowing other checks and not getting into the eye of our b3-bishop.

After castling, White is doing great here. 

Moves like Nc3 and d4 aim to open up the center against Black's uncastled king. 

Re1 will be destructive as well.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/8/P.text:
In the Traxler Counterattack, Black ignores the threat of Nxf7 and brings the bishop to c5, eyeing the soft f2-pawn.

As we've already mentioned in the previous study, Bxf7 offers a simple solution to this position.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black plays 3...Nf6, attacking the e4 pawn. This allows the Fried Liver Attack.

To enter the Fried Liver, we play 4.Ng5!, attacking f7, which is not easy to defend.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black also develops a knight while defending their pawn.

Now, 3.Bc4 is the signature move that signifies the Italian Game!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Once again, we start with 1.e4 e5.

White will now develop their kingside knight and pressure the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the second part about The Traxler! 

The main difference from the first study is that Black goes for 5...Kf8 instead of ...Ke7. 

Let's get into it!
